problem.title: Design a 10M-Metric/Sec Time-Series Database & Downsampling Engine
problem.tagline: Ingesting 10M points/sec with Gorilla in-memory chunks, inverted label indexes, and tiered S3 rollups.
problem.purpose: Design a Prometheus/Mimir-scale distributed time-series database that handles 10M samples/sec, bounds high-cardinality label index blowups, and serves both 2-hour alerting queries and 1-year dashboards in <200 ms.
problem.prompt: Design a distributed Time-Series Database ingesting 10M samples/sec across 50M active series (10s scrape interval), supporting <50 ms alerting queries over the last 2 hours, <500 ms 90-day dashboard queries, and 1-year retention.

prerequisites.title: Gorilla Time-Series Compression
prerequisites.summary: Know how 2-hour Gorilla chunks compress 16-byte `(ts, float64)` samples to ~1.37 bytes in RAM.

prerequisites.title: Inverted Indexes & Cardinality
prerequisites.summary: Understand how `label=value` posting lists map metric selectors to Series IDs—and why unbounded labels like `user_id` explode memory.

spark.summary: Shard ingestion by series hash onto Gorilla-compressed 2h in-memory Head blocks backed by WAL, flush immutable blocks to S3, and compact 10s raw points into 5m/1h downsampled rollups.
spark.keyTakeaway: When designing a 10M-metric/sec TSDB, keep hot 2-hour Gorilla chunks in sharded ingester RAM with a WAL, flush immutable blocks to object storage, and pre-compute 5m/1h downsampled rollups so long-range dashboards never scan raw 10s points.
spark.byteSummary:
At 10M samples/sec, raw ingestion is 160 MB/s (13.8 TB/day) uncompressed, and 50M active series will overwhelm any single-node B-Tree or row-oriented SQL database with random disk I/O.

The architecture splits into a stateful Ingester Head and a stateless Object-Storage Compactor/Querier: (1) Metric routers consistent-hash `(metric_name, sorted_labels)` to Ingester shards, where each series appends to a 2-hour Gorilla-compressed in-memory chunk (~1.37 B/pt) protected by a sequential Write-Ahead Log (WAL); (2) Every 2 hours, ingesters flush immutable TSDB/Parquet blocks + inverted label indexes to S3/GCS and truncate the WAL; (3) Background compactors merge blocks and generate 5-minute and 1-hour downsampled rollups (`min, max, sum, count`).

Alerting queries over the last 2 hours hit Ingester RAM directly in <50 ms, while 90-day dashboards read pre-aggregated 1h rollups from S3/Parquet in <500 ms—cutting scan volume by 360x.

learningJourney.title: R & E · Requirements, Ingestion & Retention Math
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Quantifies DRAM savings from Gorilla and scan savings from 5m/1h downsampling.

explanation.foundation: 10M samples/sec x 16 bytes uncompressed = 160 MB/sec = 13.8 TB/day = 5.04 PB/year if stored raw.
explanation.core: Illustrative Sizing: With Gorilla compression (~1.4 B/pt), 10M samples/sec = 14 MB/sec = 1.21 TB/day. A 2-hour hot Head window across 50M active series needs `14 MB/s * 7,200 s ~ 101 GB` of compressed chunk RAM (plus ~100 GB for the in-memory inverted label index -> easily served by 16–20 ingester nodes with 32 GB RAM each at RF=3).
explanation.deepDive: For a 90-day dashboard query at 10s resolution, scanning raw data requires reading `777,600` points per series; scanning a 1-hour downsampled rollup reads just `2,160` points—a 360x reduction in S3 bytes and CPU.

learningJourney.title: S · Storage: Inverted Label Index + 2h Gorilla Chunks
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Shows how `{service='api', status='500'}` resolves to Series IDs without scanning 50M series.

explanation.foundation: Users query metrics by label selectors like `http_requests_total{env='prod', region='us-east'}`. Scanning 50M series names sequentially would take seconds.
explanation.core: Each block maintains an Inverted Index: `Postings[(label_name, label_val)] -> sorted uint32[] SeriesIDs`. Querying `env='prod' AND region='us-east'` intersects two sorted posting lists in sub-millisecond time, then reads only the matching SeriesIDs' Gorilla chunks.
explanation.deepDive: Cardinality Guardrail: High-cardinality labels (`request_id`, `user_id`) blow up the inverted index. Enforce per-tenant active-series limits (e.g., max 2M active series/tenant) and drop/reject samples exceeding cardinality caps at the Distributor before they hit Ingester RAM.

sectionDiagram.title: Inverted Label Postings -> Series ID Table -> Gorilla Chunks

learningJourney.title: H & A · Write Path, Replication & Fan-Out Query Engine
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Traces ingestion durability (WAL + RF=3) and how Queriers merge hot RAM + cold S3.

explanation.foundation: Distributors receive Prometheus `remote_write` batches, enforce tenant cardinality/rate limits, and hash `(tenant_id, metric_labels)` onto a consistent-hash ring of Ingesters with RF=3.
explanation.core: Each Ingester appends incoming samples to a local sequential WAL (for crash recovery) and into the series' 2-hour Gorilla chunk. Every 2 hours, Ingesters compact the sealed Head chunk into an immutable block and upload it to S3/GCS. Queriers fan out reads in parallel: `t > now - 2h` goes to Ingesters; `t <= now - 2h` goes to Store-Gateways reading S3 blocks.
explanation.deepDive: With RF=3 and W=2, R=2 quorum writes, losing an Ingester node never drops recent metrics—and a restarted Ingester replays its local WAL in ~15–30 seconds.

sectionDiagram.title: Distributor -> Ingester (WAL + Gorilla) -> S3 Block -> Querier Merge

learningJourney.title: D · Detailed Design: Downsampling & Cardinality Protection
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Prevents OOM crashes from label explosions and speeds up 90-day queries by 360x.

explanation.foundation: When a buggy microservice accidentally puts a `trace_id` into a Prometheus label, active series count jumps from 50K to 50M in minutes—crashing Ingesters with OOM.
explanation.core: Protect Ingesters at the Distributor using a per-tenant HyperLogLog / bounded series-cache limiter: reject new series with HTTP `429` once a tenant exceeds its quota. Meanwhile, asynchronous Compactors read raw 2h S3 blocks and emit 5m and 1h rollup blocks storing `{min, max, sum, count}` per bucket.
explanation.deepDive: Why store `{sum, count}` instead of `avg`? Because averages are not associative (`avg(avg_A, avg_B) != true_avg`)! Storing `sum` and `count` lets the Querier compute exact `avg = sum(sums) / sum(counts)` across arbitrary time windows.

decisionFramework.problem: How to keep both 2-hour alerting (<50 ms) and 90-day dashboards (<500 ms) fast at 10M metrics/sec.
decisionFramework.naiveSolution: Store all 10s raw points in one database and scan raw rows for 90-day graphs.
decisionFramework.whyItFails: 90-day queries scan 777,600 points per series, saturating disk/S3 bandwidth and timing out.
decisionFramework.alternatives: Raw-only scans vs. Pre-computed `avg` rollups vs. Associative `{min, max, sum, count}` rollups.
decisionFramework.decision: Keep 2h Gorilla chunks in Ingester RAM, flush 2h blocks to S3, and compact into 5m/1h `{min, max, sum, count}` rollups.
decisionFramework.tradeOffs: Adds ~15–20% extra S3 storage for rollup tiers in exchange for 360x faster multi-month dashboard queries.

decisionExercise.prompt: A team pre-computes 1-hour rollups storing only `avg_value` per hour. When a user queries `avg_over_time` across 7 days with uneven scrape counts (some hours had 10 samples, others had 360), the dashboard shows wrong numbers. Why?

options.label: Averages are non-associative; rollups must store `sum` and `count` so the querier computes `sum(sums) / sum(counts)`.
options.explanation: Correct! Taking the mean of means weights sparse hours equally with dense hours; `{sum, count}` stays exact.

options.label: Gorilla compression only works on integers.
S3 object storage reorders hourly blocks.
options.explanation: Block ordering does not cause weighted-average math errors.

learningJourney.title: E & D · Evaluation, Assumptions, Limitations & Glossary
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Documents sizing assumptions, out-of-order tradeoffs, and TSDB terminology.

explanation.foundation: Sizing assumes a 10s regular scrape interval across 50M active series (~10M/sec) and ~1.4 bytes/point average Gorilla compression.
explanation.core: Assumptions & Limitations: If clients send heavily out-of-order samples (>2 hours late), they cannot append to the active Head chunk and must write to an Out-of-Order (OOO) head block that compacts separately on flush. Inverted index RAM scales with unique label-value pairs, requiring strict per-tenant cardinality quotas.
explanation.deepDive: Glossary: Head Block (active 2h in-memory Gorilla chunk tier); Posting List (sorted list of Series IDs matching a `label=value` pair); Cardinality Explosion (unbounded growth of unique label combinations); Associative Rollup (storing `{min, max, sum, count}` for exact re-aggregation).

steps.title: 10M/s Ingest Into 2h Gorilla Head
steps.explanation: Distributors route samples to RF=3 Ingesters; WAL guarantees durability while Gorilla compresses to 1.4 B/pt.

steps.title: 2-Hour Block Flush & 5m/1h Rollups
steps.explanation: Sealed 2h blocks flush to S3 and Compactors build associative {min, max, sum, count} rollups.

steps.title: High-Cardinality Spike Blocked
steps.explanation: Distributor catches a sudden label cardinality explosion and sheds excess new series before Ingesters OOM.

steps.title: 90-Day Dashboard Query (<500 ms)
steps.explanation: Querier merges live Head points with pre-computed 1h rollups from S3 in 185 ms.

knowledgeChecks.question: At 10M samples/sec, why does a TSDB keep 2 hours of Gorilla chunks in Ingester RAM instead of writing directly to S3 on every scrape?

options.text: S3 cannot handle 10M tiny appends/sec, and keeping 2h Gorilla chunks in RAM (~101 GB) lets alerting queries run in <50 ms.
options.feedback: Correct! Batching 2-hour chunks amortizes S3 PUTs while keeping hot alerts fast in RAM.

options.text: S3 does not support storing numbers.
options.feedback: S3 stores arbitrary binary blocks; it's the per-object latency and request rate that requires batching.

options.text: Gorilla compression only works in RAM, never on disk.
options.feedback: Gorilla chunks are flushed directly into immutable disk/S3 blocks.

options.text: To avoid using a Write-Ahead Log.
options.feedback: Ingesters still use a local sequential WAL for crash durability.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Object stores optimize for large immutable blocks, while alerting needs sub-50 ms access to recent samples.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why should downsampled TSDB rollups store `{sum, count}` rather than pre-computing `avg`?

options.text: Because `avg` is non-associative across buckets with different sample counts, whereas `sum` and `count` re-aggregate exactly.
options.feedback: Correct! `sum(sums) / sum(counts)` is mathematically exact across any window.

options.text: `avg` cannot be stored as a float64.
To double the size of the inverted index.
options.feedback: Rollups store metric values, not inverted label indexes.
PromQL supports `avg_over_time`, which relies on exact underlying aggregates.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Associative aggregates (`min`, `max`, `sum`, `count`) allow multi-tier rollups without statistical skew.

knowledgeChecks.question: Where should high-cardinality label explosions (e.g., accidentally adding `request_id` as a metric label) be stopped?

options.text: At the stateless Distributor layer via per-tenant active-series quotas before new series allocate Ingester RAM.
options.feedback: Correct! Stopping excess series at the Distributor prevents Ingester OOM crashes.

options.text: Inside the S3 Compactor 2 hours later.
options.feedback: By 2 hours later, Ingesters have already OOM-crashed.

options.text: By deleting the WAL every 5 seconds.
options.feedback: Deleting the WAL causes data loss and doesn't free active Head memory.
Without inverted indexes, label queries cannot run.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Admitting bounded series at the stateless ingress Distributor protects stateful Ingester memory.

beginner.summary: Handle 10M metrics/sec by buffering 2 hours of Gorilla-compressed data in memory, saving blocks to S3, and pre-computing 5m/1h summaries for fast long-range graphs.
beginner.keyTakeaway: When building a high-scale metrics database, compress recent data in memory with Gorilla and pre-compute hourly summaries so multi-month dashboards load fast.
beginner.byteSummary: Ingesters compress the last 2 hours of metrics in RAM (~1.4 bytes/point) with a WAL for safety, flush blocks to S3, and compact old data into 5m and 1h rollups.

intermediate.summary: Shard 50M series onto RF=3 Ingesters (WAL + 2h Gorilla Head + Inverted Index), flush to S3, and compact into associative `{min, max, sum, count}` rollups.
intermediate.keyTakeaway: When designing a 10M-metric/sec TSDB, pair 2-hour Gorilla Head blocks + inverted label indexes with Distributor cardinality quotas and associative S3 rollups.
intermediate.byteSummary: Distributors enforce per-tenant cardinality caps, Ingesters hold ~101 GB of 2h Gorilla chunks in RAM, and Compactors build 5m/1h `{min, max, sum, count}` rollups for 360x faster 90-day queries.

advanced.summary: Consistent-hashed RF=3 Ingester ring with W=2/R=2 WAL recovery, inverted posting-list intersection, OOO head handling, and associative S3 rollup compaction.
advanced.keyTakeaway: When scaling TSDBs to 10M+ samples/sec, isolate out-of-order writes from Gorilla chunks, enforce Distributor cardinality limits, and merge hot RAM + cold rollups in parallel.
advanced.byteSummary: Combining Distributor cardinality gating, RF=3 Ingesters with 2h Gorilla + OOO heads, inverted posting-list intersection, and associative `{min, max, sum, count}` S3 rollups sustains <50 ms alerts and <500 ms 90-day queries.
